title: From Pemberley to Flavortown
description: A chaotic mix of 90s PBS childhood, holiday film classics, Jane Austen heroines, foundational American history, deeply questionable snack choices, and the legends of Food Network television.

questions.question: This enormous purple dinosaur sang 'I Love You, You Love Me' while the entire adult population of America developed a mysterious aversion to the color purple.
This bespectacled aardvark from Elwood City has a sister named D.W. who is, objectively, the most chaotic character in the history of children's television.

Wearing a bow tie and enough infectious enthusiasm to make middle schoolers care about thermodynamics, this scientist-host turned PBS into the coolest channel on television for exactly 22 minutes per week.
This small Jack Russell terrier imagined himself as Romeo, Don Quixote, and Sherlock Holmes — single-handedly tricking American children into reading classic literature without realizing it.

In this 1992 PBS mystery series, Brooklyn teenagers received cryptic messages assembled from available letters by a friendly ghost — a premise that sounds haunting but was marketed to children as educational.
An 8-year-old accidentally left behind defends his house from two burglars using a series of elaborate booby traps that would — in any realistic scenario — hospitalize both men for several months.
In this 1983 holiday classic, a boy's entire Christmas wish is a Red Ryder BB gun, and virtually every adult in his life responds with a prediction about his eyes.

Will Ferrell plays a full-grown human raised by elves in this 2003 comedy — a man whose diet consists primarily of syrup-soaked cotton balls and whose social skills were clearly not part of the North Pole curriculum.

In this 1946 Frank Capra classic, a suicidal small-town banker is visited by his well-meaning but incompetent guardian angel — who earns his wings by showing the man a world without him, which goes badly for everyone.
questions.answer: What is It's a Wonderful Life?

questions.question: Clark Griswold staples 25,000 lights to his house, invites every family member he has, and completely loses his mind when Cousin Eddie parks an RV in the driveway in this beloved holiday disaster film.
questions.answer: What is National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation?

categories.name: IT IS A TRUTH UNIVERSALLY ACKNOWLEDGED

questions.question: This brooding, wealthy owner of Pemberley is Pride and Prejudice's romantic hero — whose first marriage proposal is so condescending and insulting that the woman he loves rejects him on the spot.
In this Austen novel, sensible Elinor locks her emotions away tightly while her sister Marianne cries dramatically about everything — making them history's original introvert-extrovert duo.

This Austen novel follows a well-meaning but catastrophically misguided matchmaker in the village of Highbury who meddles in everyone's love life and causes most of the problems she's supposedly trying to solve.

Austen's most whimsical novel follows a naive young woman who reads far too many Gothic horror novels, visits a creepy English country estate, and incorrectly concludes that her host murdered his late wife — making her history's first literary conspiracy theorist.

Published after Austen's death, this final completed novel follows 27-year-old Anne Elliot reconnecting with the Navy captain she was talked out of marrying years earlier — and culminates in one of English literature's most famous love letters.

In 1773, American colonists dumped 342 chests of British tea into Boston Harbor to protest taxation — an act of civil disobedience that was either a principled stand against tyranny or the most dramatic tea spill in history.
questions.answer: What is the Boston Tea Party?

questions.question: In 1803, President Thomas Jefferson purchased approximately 828,000 square miles of land from Napoleon — doubling the size of the United States for roughly four cents per acre.

This 19th-century doctrine — the belief that the United States was divinely destined to expand westward across the continent — was excellent news for American settlers and considerably less excellent for the people already living there.
Issued on January 1, 1863, Abraham Lincoln's landmark executive order declared all enslaved people in Confederate states 'shall be then, thenceforward, and forever free.'

Beginning with a 1972 burglary at the Democratic National Committee headquarters, this political scandal led to the only presidential resignation in American history, when Richard Nixon left office in August 1974.

America's best-selling cookie since 1912 has inspired a decades-long debate about the correct consumption method — twist, lick, or dunk — and the answer is that all three are valid and anyone who disagrees is wrong.
These fluorescent-orange triangular chips leave a powdery residue on your fingers that has destroyed more keyboards, game controllers, and white shirts than any other snack in recorded history.

A British court once ruled these saddle-shaped stackable crisps contain so little actual potato that they legally do not qualify as a potato chip in the United Kingdom — a distinction that changed nobody's purchasing habits.

These rectangular pastry-filled toaster treats — sold in flavors ranging from strawberry to birthday cake to 'Unfrosted' — have been marketed as a breakfast food since 1964, which remains America's most optimistic nutritional claim.

Despite being consistently voted America's least favorite Halloween candy and universally described as waxy and vaguely wrong, this triangular autumn staple still sells 35 million pounds per year — making it either beloved or haunted.

This frosted-tipped, board-short-wearing Food Network host has declared himself mayor of a municipality called Flavortown and visits local restaurants with the enthusiasm of someone who has never had a bad meal in his life.

This 'Barefoot Contessa' has built an empire on cooking for her husband Jeffrey and reassuring viewers that store-bought is fine — while quietly requiring that everything be made with 'really good' olive oil that costs $47 at a specialty shop.

This bow-tie-wearing food scientist turned 'Good Eats' into a chemistry lecture disguised as cooking TV, explaining why bread rises while making viewers feel personally responsible for every bad meal they've ever made.

This perpetually competitive chef has won Iron Chef, launched more New York restaurants than most people have had jobs, and hosted a show where he showed up unannounced to challenge fellow chefs on their own turf.
Food Network's original superstar, this New Orleans-inspired chef shouted 'BAM!' and 'Kick it up a notch!' into America's living rooms long enough to make his Essence spice blend a household name.
